paper_metadata.title: Integration of parameterized quantum circuits within classical neural network for financial time-series prediction

summary: The paper proposes a hybrid classical–quantum neural network with a parameterized quantum circuit (up to 8 qubits and 3 layers) for credit‑default prediction on the Kaggle American Express dataset (5,531,451 records, 458,913 customers). The model achieves about 0.88 accuracy with final cross‑entropy loss ≈0.2157 and reports training time of 453.3 s, compared with 4991.3 s (XGBoost), 3985.4 s (LightGBM), and 3884.2 s (CatBoost). All experiments are executed via classical simulation on a CPU rather than quantum hardware.

experiments.description: Hybrid classical-quantum neural network for credit card default prediction using a parameterized quantum circuit, evaluated across varying qubit counts (5-8), optimizer choices, and circuit depths (1-3 layers) on a large time-series financial dataset.

algorithm.variant: dressed quantum circuit / hybrid neural network with parameterized quantum circuit
algorithm.ansatz: RY rotations followed by CNOT entangling layer
algorithm.optimizer: Adam; RMSprop; RMSprop with momentum; Adamax
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained for 20 epochs until loss stabilized
algorithm.parameter_initialization: rotation angles initialized with random angles

problem_formulation.encoding_details: classical features are preprocessed by a classical layer and encoded into quantum states via RY rotations; one rotation parameter per qubit per layer
problem_formulation.objective_function: binary cross-entropy loss for credit default prediction

problem_instance.description: Credit card default prediction on a time-series financial dataset from the American Express Kaggle competition

dataset_specification.preprocessing: EDA, normalization, missing-value handling by imputation or feature omission, one-hot encoding, chi-square feature selection to top 64 features, random 60:40 train-test split

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Exploratory data analysis; normalization; missing values imputed or omitted depending on feature importance; categorical variables one-hot encoded; top 64 features selected using Chi score method; dataset partitioned into 276 mini-batches of 1000 examples
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: single random 60:40 train-test split; performance reported on training and test sets using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score; loss curves over 20 epochs

implementation_details.classical_solver: gradient-based optimizers; classical baselines XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: normalization, missing-value handling, one-hot encoding, chi-square feature selection
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: sigmoid output layer for binary classification

speedup_claims.factor: about 8.6x faster than XGBoost; about 8.8x faster than LightGBM; about 8.6x faster than CatBoost
speedup_claims.conditions: training on the same time-series financial dataset
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a wall-clock training-time comparison only; no asymptotic complexity proof or hardware-normalized benchmark is provided.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not specified; experiments executed on classical CPU with simulated PQC up to 8 qubits and 3 layers.
limiting_factors: No execution on actual quantum hardware; all results obtained via classical simulation
Very small quantum system size (≤8 qubits)
Reported speedup is only wall‑clock training time compared to classical boosting implementations
Quantum circuit is embedded inside a classical neural network so overall computation remains classical
Large classical preprocessing and feature selection pipeline dominates computation

notes: Hardware is not tied to a named QPU or simulator; only Google Colab Pro / CPU environment is reported, so hardware.type remains not_specified.
The paper reports qubit counts 5, 6, 7, and 8; the maximum configuration (8 qubits) is recorded in quantum_resources.num_qubits, with scalability data captured in hyperparameters.
Circuit depth is reported as 1, 2, and 3 layers; the maximum configuration (3 layers) is recorded in quantum_resources.circuit_depth.
Training-time comparison is reported against classical gradient-boosting baselines; no asymptotic complexity proof is given, so speedup_order is none_proven.
The authors suggest improved efficiency and faster training compared with gradient boosting methods, but this is only an empirical wall‑clock comparison on a classical CPU.
No theoretical quantum speedup or complexity improvement is demonstrated.
Because the PQC is simulated classically and the system size is ≤8 qubits, this does not constitute quantum advantage under Hoefler et al. criteria.
